title: Backups You Can Actually Restore
intro: Nobody needs backups; everybody needs restores. A backup is only real once it has been restored and checked. This tutorial uses restic (encrypted, deduplicated backups to S3 or any object store) plus a database-consistent dump, and ends with the step most teams skip: a test restore.

steps.prompt: Databases can't be backed up safely by copying their live data files. Dump the database 'shop' in PostgreSQL's custom format to /backup/shop.dump.
steps.explanation: A consistent snapshot of the database, as of the moment the dump started.
steps.why: Copying /var/lib/postgresql while postgres runs produces files from different moments, which can fail to start or silently lose data on restore. pg_dump (or the database's own snapshot and backup tools) gives a consistent copy. Custom format (-Fc) is compressed and allows selective restores.

steps.prompt: Back up /etc and /backup to the restic repository in $RESTIC_REPOSITORY.
steps.fake_output:
Files:          14 new,  1203 changed, 18112 unmodified
Added to the repository: 412.117 MiB (398.020 MiB stored)
processed 19329 files, 2.611 GiB in 0:41
snapshot 7f3c2a1b saved
steps.explanation: Only 412MiB of new data was uploaded, thanks to deduplication.
steps.why: restic encrypts client-side, deduplicates across snapshots, and writes to object storage. Keep backups in a different account or region from production, with object lock or versioning, so ransomware or a stolen admin credential can't delete production and its backups together.

steps.prompt: List the snapshots in the repository.
steps.why: Pair this with a retention policy ('restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --prune'), or storage grows forever. The oldest snapshot you keep decides how far back you can recover, for example from corruption discovered two weeks late.

steps.fake_output:
using temporary cache in /tmp/restic-check-cache-123
load indexes
check all packs
check snapshots, trees and blobs
no errors were found
steps.why: 'check' validates the repository's structure; '--read-data' also reads back every byte, which is slower. Neither proves the backup contains what you need: only a restore does.

steps.prompt: Do the restore test: restore the latest snapshot into /tmp/restore-test.
steps.fake_output:
restoring <Snapshot 7f3c2a1b of [/etc /backup] at 2026-09-28 10:58:51> to /tmp/restore-test
Summary: Restored 19329 files/dirs (2.611 GiB) in 0:38
steps.why: Restore to a scratch location, never over production, and time it: that duration is your real recovery time (RTO), which is often very different from what's written in the disaster-recovery plan.

steps.prompt: Finally, prove the database dump is usable: restore /tmp/restore-test/backup/shop.dump into a scratch database shop_restore_test.
steps.fake_output:
(no output: restore completed)
$ psql shop_restore_test -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM orders;'
  count
---------
 1882461
steps.explanation: The restored database opens, and its row counts match expectations.
steps.why: This is the step that makes the backup real. Automate the whole restore test (restore, start, run sanity queries) weekly, and alert when it fails. Teams that don't only find out their backups are broken during the disaster (servers-incident-006).
